t: Stop Lecturing Students And Lower Your Stress tudents-and-lower-your-stress/
q: It is my belief that the number one cause of stress among teachers is a reliance on one’s words to try to convince students to behave as desired—i.e., lecturing students as a method of classroom management.
Lecturing individual students isn’t an effective classroom management strategy because it doesn’t work in the long run, it creates resentment in your students, and it’s stressful to you.
Listening to your criticism is the consequence. If they can weather your lecture, they know they will be free from further consequence when it’s over.
Why a student breaks a rule is, in most circumstances, irrelevant. Very few students, or adults for that matter, are able to articulate why they made a bad choice.
Arguing with students lowers your leadership stature and authority to the same level of the student—which it is not. You are the teacher and leader in the classroom and you make the decisions.
Rules are rules. Other than for the purpose of gathering information, there is nothing to talk about. If a student breaks a rule, you give him or her a consequence and move on.
What does work is following your classroom management plan exclusively. Lecturing doesn’t support your plan; it hinders it.

Replacing individual lecturing with consistent enforcement of stated consequences is presented as both more effective for changing behavior and less stressful for teachers.
Students often experience a one-on-one lecture as the consequence itself -- if they can 'weather' the lecture, they expect no further consequence to follow.
Interrogating students about why they misbehaved is largely futile, since most people cannot articulate the reasons behind a bad choice, and pushing for answers risks provoking arguments.

t: Are You Using This Power Word? -power-word/
q: I was eating a banana as I began to push through the turnstile, when a man in a red windbreaker, presumably security, stopped me and said, “Sir, you can’t bring that banana into the stadium.
As it turns out, that something has strong implications when it comes to classroom management and can possibly be the difference between success and failure with your students.

Dr. Robert B. Cialdini describes several experiments that prove overwhelmingly that when we ask someone to do something—or not to do something—the response will be much more favorable if we provide a compelling reason.
It’s interesting to note, however, that experimenters discovered that even when the reasons offered were poor—to the point of absurdity—most subjects were still agreeable to the request.

If your students go to time-out and are angry with you or are complaining about your decision, then you’re doing something wrong. Often, it’s because you’re not using the word because and then following with cogent reasons.
Classroom management doesn’t have to be demanding or dictatorial to be effective—and it shouldn’t be—but it does need to be smart.

A recommended three-step method for enforcing classroom rules: state the consequence, name the rule broken, then give a compelling reason using 'because.'
Psychologist Robert Cialdini's research shows people comply far more readily with requests when given a reason introduced by the word 'because,' even when the reason offered is weak.

t: Broken Windows Theory And Classroom Management nagement/
q: The broken windows theory of crime prevention postulates that disorder is an invitation for crime to occur. If the environment of a particular neighborhood triggers the belief that no one cares or that no one is in charge, then crime in that neighborhood goes up.

Just as enforcing minor quality-of-life crimes can benefit cities and neighborhoods, enforcing classroom rule violations that many teachers perceive to be not worth the time are, in fact, very much worth the time.
Small details that for many teachers don’t seem to be worth the effort can have a strong impact on the behavior of your students.

Too many teachers wait until a rule is broken in a big way before enforcing it. This is a mistake in the highest order. It’s confusing to students to have rules on a sliding scale, dependent upon your mood, who the student is, or how severely the rule was broken.

The fact is, this is a wonderful opportunity. That the student is one of your best is perfect. It’s an opportunity to show all of your students that rules will be enforced no matter what, no matter when, and no matter who is breaking them.
Test the broken windows theory in your own classroom by enforcing even the little things—minor infractions that at first seem inconsequential, but in reality, are the most important.
x: Malcolm Gladwell's 'broken windows theory' of crime reduction is applied to classroom management: small visible signs of disorder invite larger, more frequent misbehavior.
The core prescription is to enforce even minor, seemingly inconsequential classroom management rules precisely and consistently, without exception.

He applies this directly to classroom management using the image of a messy row of student backpacks, arguing that tolerating small signs of disorder and disrespect sends the same 'no one is watching' signal to students…
Waiting to enforce a rule until it's broken 'in a big way' creates a confusing, inconsistent sliding scale of enforcement that invites students to test limits.
Even well-behaved students breaking minor rules (e.g., calling out without raising a hand) should be held to the same standard, since selective enforcement undermines the whole plan.
The piece closes with a direct challenge to test the broken windows theory by enforcing even minor classroom infractions consistently.

t: One Classroom Management Strategy For Every Student very-student/
q: Some of my classroom management solutions run counter to what many teachers are doing, and in the case of students who repeatedly disrupt the classroom, this is also true. For example, I don’t speak more often to misbehaving-prone students or give them more attention than I would any other student.
Giving more attention to troublesome students increases the likelihood that their unwanted behavior will continue. Yet, in my experience, this seems to be the preferred method.

When you attend to poorly behaved students more often, you’re communicating to them in a subtle but clear way that they’re different, that they don’t have what it takes to control themselves like other students.
So what is the solution? Ignore the behavior and hope it goes away? Tiptoe around the student(s) and hope they aren’t too disruptive? No, the solution is to treat them just like everyone else.
When you begin using this strategy, the first couple of weeks or so may be tough. One or more of your students may be in time-out a lot, they may act out more than usual and more dramatically.

In my experience, those students with disruptive tendencies love this style of classroom management. It’s fair, and because it isn’t arbitrary or based on personal feelings, it completely removes tension between the student and his or her teacher.

Giving chronically disruptive students extra attention, discussion, or special handling is argued to reinforce their unwanted behavior rather than reduce it.
Excess attention communicates to struggling students that they are fundamentally different and unable to control themselves, damaging self-esteem over time.

His proposed alternative is to apply the classroom management plan to disruptive students exactly as it applies to everyone else -- delivering the same consequences, offering the same ordinary praise, and refusing to…
Teachers should expect a difficult one-to-two week transition period, with increased time-outs and more dramatic behavior, before the strategy shows results.
Disruptive students reportedly respond well to this consistent, unemotional approach because it removes tension and confusion from their relationship with the teacher.

t: Sending Students To The Office Will Weaken Your Ability To Manage Your Classroom your-ability-to-manage-your-classroom/
q: In nearly 20 years of teaching, I’ve never sent one of my students to the office because of a behavior issue.
It is simply a byproduct of my strong belief that every time you send a student to someone else for a behavior issue (i.e., the principal, vice-principal, or counselor), you weaken your authority.
Witnessing a fight, being challenged and cursed at, and learning a student has brought a weapon to school are all examples of behavior that must be overseen by an administrator.
Every time you send a student to the office, you’re communicating to your students that you don’t have full command of your classroom.

Principals are too busy to monitor students placed in time-out around the office, so they must rely on stern lectures and assurance from the student that the behavior will change. Both are weak methods of behavior management.

It’s important to note, however, that it is an authority that engenders respect (i.e., an authoritative style), not resentment, which is often produced from an authoritarian style of classroom management.

t: Supercharge Your Classroom Management Plan With Detailed Modeling plan-through-modeling/
q: Modeling is so effective that it should be among your most often used teaching strategies.
However, you can supercharge the effectiveness of what you’re modeling, regardless of what it is, by adding an important element: explicit detail.
It’s the peripheral stuff–the stuff that teachers typically don’t model–that is the most important and will make the greatest difference to your teaching.
Students’ knowing what is expected of them is a critical part of any successful classroom management plan, and detailed modeling does just that. Too many teachers are vague in this regard.

To model calling out, the teacher might sit at a student’s desk while a student plays the part of the teacher. This gives the teacher the opportunity to demonstrate the rudeness, and even absurdity, of interrupting someone who is speaking.
Merely explaining classroom rules, or anything else for that matter, is minimally effective. Students must actively participate in and experience what it means to break rules.
Nothing is as effective as detailed modeling in communicating anything important to your students… nothing.

Adding explicit, realistic detail to ordinary modeling -- rather than performing a task generically at the front of the room -- significantly increases its effectiveness.

t: The Not-So-Secret To Effective Classroom Management anagement/
q: They test drive interactive bulletin boards, ever-new sets of rules and consequences, echoing chants, bells, and other attention-getting devices, and time-consuming community circles.

99% of teachers have rules or standards of behavior for their classroom, and most of these teachers have consequences in case these rules are broken. This is good. But here is the problem: only a small percentage of teachers actually follow their rules and consequences to the letter.
The central reason why so many teachers struggle with classroom management is because they don’t really follow their plan. Most only kinda-sorta do.

Every time you let something go, ignore a broken rule, or fail to enforce a rule with a consequence, you are letting your students know that you don’t really mean what you say, that you can’t be counted on or trusted.
In the beginning of the school year or if you’re starting over, it’s a good idea to review your plan daily for the first four to six weeks.

And here is the best part: it’s not personal. Because you’re following your plan and delivering on the promise you gave your students, there will be no more need for less effective and potentially hurtful methods like lecturing, arguing, or raising your voice.
